lines.text: Take two pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. If their edges fit perfectly, you know at once that they were cut from the same picture.
Now open an old atlas. Look at the coast of South America, and then at the coast of Africa, across the ocean.
The bulge of Brazil tucks neatly into the hollow of West Africa, like two puzzle pieces that someone has pulled apart.
But a puzzle can be torn apart. Can a planet? Could whole continents once have been joined, and then drifted across the world?
The ground under our feet is the one thing we trust never to move. And if it does move, it moves far too slowly to see.
So how did we find out? From a torn map, a little reptile, a man who died on the ice… and stripes hidden at the bottom of the sea.
Imagine a rock sitting in a meadow. Grass grows round it, trees rise, a whole town is built… and the rock has barely crept a step.
Nobody could ever watch that happen. A human life is far too short, and the motion is far too slow.
For centuries, people noticed that the coasts matched. Most called it a coincidence. Then one man refused to let it go.
His name was Alfred Wegener. He was not a geologist at all. He studied the weather, sending balloons high into the sky.
From high above, the land below looks like a map spread out on a table. And Wegener could not stop looking at maps.
He saw the matching coasts. Later he wrote that it was like tearing a newspaper, and then fitting the torn pieces back together.
If the edges fit, and the lines of print run straight on across the tear, you could be sure the pieces were one page. But where was the print?
So he went looking for the lines of print. Not on paper, but in the rocks and fossils on both sides of the ocean.
In 1912 he said it out loud. The continents had once been joined in one giant land, and had slowly drifted apart.
Later that giant land got a name: Pangaea, from the Greek for ‘all the earth’.
Picture all the continents stitched together like a patchwork quilt, with seams where the oceans would one day open.
And on that quilt, the print runs on across the seams. Take Mesosaurus: a small, slim reptile with a long snout that swam in fresh water.
Its bones are found in southern Africa and in South America, and nowhere else on Earth. How could that be?
A freshwater swimmer could never cross a salty ocean thousands of kilometres wide. So how did it live on both sides?
Unless, when it was alive, there was no ocean between them at all: just one lake, one shore, one land.
Then there is a plant called Glossopteris, a seed fern with leaves shaped like tongues. Its fossils turn up in South America, Africa, India, Australia…
…and Antarctica. A plant of mild, green forests, buried under the ice at the bottom of the world.
Like a fern in a freezer. Either the climate had flipped completely, or Antarctica had once sat somewhere much warmer.
Matching coasts, matching fossils. To Wegener, the torn newspaper read straight across the tear.
But the experts were not convinced. Most geologists rejected the idea, and many of them mocked it.
Their question was simple, and it was a good one. What force could push a whole continent through the solid floor of the ocean?
Wegener had no good answer. It sounded like claiming a ship could sail straight through rock. His idea began to sink.
He didn’t give up. He kept improving his book, and he kept going back to the place he loved most: the Greenland ice.
In 1930 he led an expedition onto the ice cap, hauling supplies to a camp in the middle of Greenland through storms of terrible cold.
In November, on the way back from that camp, he never arrived. His body was found the next year, under the snow.
He had just turned fifty. Nobody knew it yet, but he died decades before anyone could prove that he had been right.
For thirty years his idea lay buried too, like a seed under the snow, waiting for proof from the last place anyone looked.
That place was the bottom of the sea. In the 1950s, the deep ocean floor was almost as unknown as the far side of the Moon.
Ships began to explore it. They sent pings of sound into the deep, and towed instruments behind them on long cables.
One of those instruments was a magnetometer: a kind of super-sensitive compass that feels how strongly the rocks below are magnetic.
As the ship sailed, a pen on board drew a wiggly line. And when the wiggles were put on a map, they made something nobody expected.
Stripes. Long bands of stronger and weaker magnetism lying across the sea floor, like the black and white keys of a piano.
And they ran alongside a great underwater mountain chain, the mid-ocean ridge, which winds round the planet like the seam on a ball.
Stranger still, the stripes on one side of the ridge were a mirror image of the stripes on the other.
Fold the map along the ridge, and the pattern lands on itself, stripe for stripe.
Why would the sea floor be striped? And why the same on both sides, like the wings of a butterfly?
In 1963, two scientists in Cambridge, Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews, saw what the stripes meant. And it changed everything.
Every so often, Earth’s magnetic field flips. North becomes south. A compass would swing round and point the other way.
At the ridge, hot melted rock wells up from below, cools, and locks in the direction of the field, like music recorded onto a tape.
Then it’s pushed aside by newer rock, and newer, out to both sides. The sea floor is a tape recorder, playing out in two directions.
So that is why the sea floor is striped: the stripes are the flips, written into stone. The ocean floor is being made right now, and it is moving.
If the sea floor moves, the continents ride along with it. They don’t plough through the ocean; they travel with it, like boxes on a conveyor belt.
Wegener was right that the continents move. He was wrong only about how. The Earth’s outer shell is cracked into giant moving plates.
Where plates pull apart, new sea floor is born. Where they push together, one dives deep under the other, and the ground shakes.
Where two continents crash, the land crumples like a rug shoved against a wall. That is how the Himalaya were born.
And the Atlantic, where Wegener first saw the tear, is still opening today, along the seam where South America and Africa came apart.
We can measure it now from space. Satellites send signals to markers bolted into rock on each continent, and time them precisely.
The answer: a few centimetres every year. About as fast as your fingernails grow.
Too slow to see. But give it two hundred million years, and that fingernail’s width became a whole ocean.
And it hasn’t stopped. Far in the future the continents will fit together again in a new way, a puzzle no one has ever seen.
Alfred Wegener never saw the proof. But the torn edges he noticed in an old atlas were real. The world really had been pulled apart.
The ground under your feet is moving right now. Slowly, quietly, about as fast as your fingernails grow… and it always has.
